pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction (8 + 3 by counting on 9,10,11; 12 − 3 by counting back 11,10,9). Ages 6–7, the bridge from counting-all to more efficient calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero' and count on/back; underpins Y2 mental strategies.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5 'Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g. by counting on 2 to add 2)'; a stepping stone toward 1.OA.6 strategies.
• Operational details: teach counting ON from the larger number (start at 8, not 1) as more efficient than counting-all, and counting BACK for subtraction, tracking the number of steps. Best supported on a number line/track so the steps are visible and the child doesn't count the start as a step. This is a transitional strategy — valued, then increasingly replaced by known facts and derived facts.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds 8 + 3 by counting on from 8. Tier B (age 7) — counts back accurately for 12 − 3 and starts count-on from the larger addend for 2 + 9. Tier C (age 7+) — explains counting on as adding and chooses count-on vs count-back sensibly.
bestPractices: Teach counting ON from the larger addend, not counting all from one, as the efficiency step.
Use a number line or number track so jumps are visible and the start number isn't miscounted as a step.
Track the number of steps with fingers or marks to prevent off-by-one errors.
Model counting back for subtraction and connect it to 'one less each time'.
Treat counting on/back as a transitional strategy — celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts for efficiency.
keyRepresentations: Number line / number track with hops
Fingers used to keep track of the count of steps
commonMisconceptions: Counting all from one instead of counting on from a number (a normal earlier stage).
Counting the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → 8,9,10 = 10), an off-by-one error.
Counting on from the first-written number rather than the larger one, making more steps than needed.
Counting in the wrong direction for subtraction.
Over-relying on counting for facts that should become instant recall.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, teach counting on for addition and counting back for subtraction as the efficiency step beyond counting-all. The core skills: start from the larger number (e.g. begin at 8 for 8+3), say the NEXT number as the first count ('9'), and track the number of steps so the start isn't miscounted. Best anchored on a visible number line/track where hops are seen and counted, then gradually replaced by known and derived facts. Target sums: 8+3=11 (count on), 12−3=9 (count back), 2+9 (start from the larger addend, 9).

activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
feedback: If a child counts the start number as the first step (8+3 → '8,9,10' = 10), point out that 8 is where you START, and the first hop lands on 9 — count the landings, not the starting spot.
If a child starts at 1 and counts everything, gently cover the first group, say '8', and count on from there; this earlier stage matures with number sense, so model rather than drill.
For subtraction going the wrong way, link counting back to 'one less each time' and track the backward hops with fingers.
If a child always starts from the first-written number (2 for 2+9), ask which number gives fewer hops and why starting at 9 is quicker.
activities.rationale: Counting on/back is literally movement along a number line, so a track where hops are visible and counted is intended to make the strategy and the off-by-one error observable, so the child can self-correct. A live track that counts each landing (and does not count the start as a step) is intended to target the classic '8,9,10'=10 slip. Starting-number highlighting, count-on/count-back modes, and a 'start from the bigger number' prompt for commutative pairs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete. Efficacy of this interaction is a proposal, not a tested result.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers to 20 including zero, using counting strategies.
1.OA.5 relates counting to addition and subtraction, e.g. counting on 2 to add 2.
Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.

activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start
feedback: Watch for an off-by-one answer (10 for 8+3): the result is 11 — recount the landings, not the start.
If the chosen start for 2+9 is 2, note that starting at 9 means only two hops instead of nine.
For 6+2, start at 6 and count on '7, 8' — two hops lands on 8.
activities.rationale: Fixed items give good spaced consolidation but cannot correct the count as it happens, so they work best after the live hopping activity rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.

activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
feedback: If the explanation defends counting all from one, model covering the first group and counting on, and ask which took fewer counts.
Praise explanations that connect counting on to adding and counting back to 'one less each time'.
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning reveals the underlying strategy and lets a tutor probe the counting-all habit; it complements, rather than replaces, watched practice where the procedure is performed and tracked.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.

constraints: Counting on/back is a transitional strategy: celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts so it isn't over-relied on for instant-recall facts.

Counting-all from one is a normal earlier developmental stage; model counting on but do not drill it as an error — children typically move beyond it as number sense grows with experience and modelling.
A static worked number line can anchor what counting on looks like but gives no practice tracking one's own steps, where the errors occur; use it as an anchor, not the main practice.
Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the choice of start number but do not elicit the child independently performing and tracking the count; pair them with doing and narrating.
Watching HOW the child counts is central: the overt count reveals strategy and off-by-one errors that the final answer alone can hide.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source row flagged the US CCSS 1.OA.5 claim and the Cognitively Guided Instruction claim as verified:false; treat their cited support as unconfirmed even though they are topically relevant.

The original rated a 3D treatment 'poor' asserting '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim is not established by the row and has been dropped. A number line is naturally one-dimensional, which is a sufficient rationale without claiming 3D is universally useless.
Arithmetic checked: 8+3=11, 12−3=9, 2+9=11, 6+2=8; the off-by-one distractor (10 for 8+3) is correctly flagged as an error, not a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why did you start counting at 8 and not at 1?
Show me on the number line how you got 12 − 3.
Which is quicker for 8 + 3 — counting everything, or counting on? Why?
For 2 + 9, which number would you start from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 11; 9; 8. Watch for the child counting ON from the larger number (starting at 8, saying '9, 10, 11'), counting BACK for the subtraction, and NOT counting the start number as a step.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts all from one rather than counting on from a number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or correct as an error — this stage self-resolves with number sense; gently model covering the first set, saying '8', and counting on, and let it mature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 8 + 3, starts at 1 and counts out all eight then all three.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → '8, 9, 10' = 10).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Start the count on the NEXT number; use a number line and fingers so the start isn't a step. Not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 10; observed saying the start number as step one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back unreliably or in the wrong direction for subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model back-counting on a number line and link to 'one less each time'; track steps with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 12 − 3 counts up, or miscounts the backward steps.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all from one, or cannot track the count reliably; frequent errors.
responseLevels.full: Counts on from the larger addend and counts back accurately, tracking the number of steps, and explains counting on as a way of adding.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on/back but with off-by-one slips, or always starts from the first-written number rather than the larger.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show me how you count each one: 8 + 3; 12 − 3; 6 + 2.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child counts is the whole test: a counting-all child starts at 1 and counts every item; a counting-on child starts at 8. An off-by-one child audibly counts the start number as step one and lands on 10. The overt count reveals the strategy and the classic error in a way the answer alone cannot.
